purpose: Sucralfate is used to treat and prevent ulcers in the stomach and the upper part of the small intestine. It helps relieve the pain and discomfort caused by these ulcers and allows them to heal. Your doctor may also prescribe it to protect the stomach lining from irritation.
how_it_works: When you swallow sucralfate, it reacts with the acid in your stomach and turns into a thick, paste-like coating. This coating sticks directly to the ulcer or irritated area like a protective bandage, shielding it from stomach acid, bile, and digestive juices. By protecting the damaged area, it gives your body the chance to heal itself naturally.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is constipation, which happens in some people. You might also notice a dry mouth, upset stomach, nausea, dizziness, or a mild headache. These side effects are usually not serious and often improve as your body adjusts to the medication.
warnings: Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, because sucralfate contains aluminum which can build up in your body if your kidneys do not work well. This medication can interfere with the absorption of many other drugs, so always take sucralfate at least 2 hours before or after your other medications. Let your doctor know if you are pregnant, breastfeeding, or have diabetes, as the liquid form contains sugar.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 1 gram (one tablet or 10 mL of liquid) taken four times a day — once before each meal and once at bedtime. It works best when taken on an empty stomach, about 30 to 60 minutes before eating. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions, and finish the full course of treatment even if you start feeling better.
